title: A seminormal ring is reduced, and so is an absolutely weakly normal ring

standard_prerequisites.name: The defining property of seminormality: for a ring A, whenever elements a and b satisfy a squared equals b cubed, there is an element c with c cubed equal to a and c squared equal to b
standard_prerequisites.source_reference: Used at proof lines 12324-12328, where the property is applied with a nilpotent element and zero
standard_prerequisites.use: It is the property that a nilpotent would violate.

standard_prerequisites.name: A ring is reduced exactly when it has no nonzero element whose square is zero
standard_prerequisites.use: Turns the failure of seminormality for a nilpotent into the reducedness assertion.

standard_prerequisites.name: Absolutely weakly normal rings are seminormal
standard_prerequisites.source_reference: Used at statement lines 12318-12322 for the 'a fortiori' clause
standard_prerequisites.use: Transfers the reducedness conclusion to absolutely weakly normal rings.

core_obligations: Assume a ring contains a nonzero element whose square is zero, so that the square of that element equals the cube of zero (proof lines 12324-12326).

Apply the defining property of seminormality to this pair: it would give an element whose cube is the nilpotent and whose square is zero, which is impossible because a cube vanishing element forces the element to vanish (proof lines 12326-12328).

Conclude that no nonzero square-zero element exists, so the ring is reduced, and the same conclusion holds for absolutely weakly normal rings because they are seminormal (proof lines 12328 and the statement's clause).
proof_roadmap: Test the seminormality property on a square-zero element to derive a contradiction, hence reducedness (proof lines 12324-12328).
difficulty_reason: The lemma says that seminormal rings and schemes are reduced and that absolutely weakly normal ones are as well (statement lines 12318-12322). The counted proof is a short direct argument: a nonzero element whose square is zero has its square equal to the cube of zero, so the defining property of seminormality would produce an element with zero square and a nilpotent cube, which is impossible (proof lines 12324-12328). It is H2: the argument is complete in the counted span and is deliberately short, and it is not dressed up as difficult.
